analysis.one_liner: Bans publicly traded corporations from spending money on federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for any company whose stock is traded on a public stock exchange, or any company it controls, to spend money on federal elections — no donations to candidates, no donations to committees, and no political ads. It would also be illegal for anyone to ask for or take such money. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it went to the Senate committee that handles election rules and stayed there until the two-year session of Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would see corporate money out of federal elections. It would also help candidates and campaigns that cannot attract corporate dollars, since they would no longer face opponents backed by unlimited corporate spending.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any publicly traded corporation, or any company under its control, to give money or anything of value in connection with a federal election, or to run political ads attacking or supporting candidates [S2] [S3].
Also makes it a violation for any person to solicit, accept, or receive corporate election money, closing the receiving end of the pipeline [S2] [S3].
Blocks corporations from routing money to committees that accept donations violating federal campaign limits, an anti-evasion measure aimed at super PAC-style vehicles [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and the political committees funded by corporate money would lose their ability to spend on federal elections, and executives who steer that spending would lose a channel of influence.
analysis.who_pays_short: Publicly traded corporations and corporate-funded committees

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only publicly traded companies. Privately held companies and their owners would keep every spending channel, creating an uneven rule that treats two large donors differently [S3].

A ban on corporate election spending runs directly against the Supreme Court's Citizens United line of cases, which protects independent corporate political spending as speech, so the bill would face immediate constitutional challenge and likely court defeat [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would remove a large flow of corporate money from federal elections, which most voters favor in principle. But the design is narrow (it spares privately held companies) and the constitutional obstacle is serious, so its practical effect would depend on courts and enforcement that the bill does not address. As written, it is a statement of principle more than a workable law — and Congress never tested it even to that point.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Rules Committee, which never held a hearing or brought it up, and the session of Congress ended with it still sitting there.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the bill on October 31, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration [S1] [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no committee hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill, so it had no bipartisan backing that might have pushed it forward [S4].
The two-year 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died automatically and any new version would have to start over from scratch [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations, because unlimited corporate election spending continued untouched. Senate leadership and the Rules Committee also avoided a floor fight over an issue neither party moved on.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; no other senator joined him

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-MN)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the fourteen months after referral

against.name: 48 of 52 Senate Democrats and Independents
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill, leaving it without a bipartisan bloc that could force committee action

sides.party_line_note: Limiting corporate money in elections is usually framed as a Democratic issue, yet the only sponsor was a conservative Republican and not one Democrat or Republican signed on, so the bill had no visible coalition on either side.

industries.note: The bill would strip listed companies of the right to spend on federal elections through contributions and ads. Their interest in continuing that spending runs against voters' interest in elections not shaped by corporate money [S3].

industries.industry: Corporate-funded political committees and super PACs
industries.note: The bill bars publicly traded corporations from giving to any committee that takes money outside federal campaign limits, cutting off a major revenue channel for these groups [S3].
